public_rationale: O'Reilly reported on June 9, 2026 that GitHub Copilot introduced usage-based billing on June 1, making previously subsidized workloads subject to metered credits. [e1] Tom's Hardware reported on June 13, 2026 that firms were using cheaper models and open-source alternatives to reduce costs. [e2] Neither report establishes the required chain: independently identified discount-dependent startups, higher effective prices, continued Big Tech support for their providers, and resulting operating viability or failure. [e1, e2]
limitations: The billing report does not identify startups made unable to sustain operations by the change. [e1]
Reported substitution does not establish sustained viability for an independently identified group of discount-dependent startups. [e2]
The reports do not match continued Big Tech funding of providers to affected startups and their operating outcomes. [e1, e2]

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Even if Big Tech keeps funding the boom, that won't help the startups, used to discounted rates, that won't be able to afford to run their companies when prices rise.
conditions: if AI model prices rise from discounted rates
the startups that won't be able to afford it

statement.excerpt: Even though Big Tech could keep funding this boom — after all, they’re pretty much entirely responsible for its existence — that won’t help the startups that won't be able to afford to run their companies, after getting used to discounted rates.

from_speaker: Big Tech could keep funding this boom
won't be able to afford to run their companies
after getting used to discounted rates
our_interpretation: The surrounding passage makes this conditional on providers raising previously discounted prices.
The ordinary reading concerns startups whose operating viability depends on those discounts. The affected group must be identified independently of whether its members subsequently fail.
Continued funding of AI providers is distinct from direct financial assistance to an affected startup.
The claim predicts an operating-affordability problem caused by higher model costs, rather than merely predicting that some AI startups will close.
criteria.support_condition: Identified startups dependent on discounted model access become unable to sustain operations because those rates rise, despite continued Big Tech support for the relevant providers.
criteria.contradiction_condition: For an independently identified affected group, records show that continued Big Tech support preserves viable operations after the relevant discounts end, defeating the predicted affordability mechanism.

evidence.excerpt: A workload that had been quietly subsidized under a flat rate started showing up as an itemized bill.
evidence.explanation: This describes a relevant subsidy-withdrawal mechanism. It does not identify startups made unviable by it or establish the complete antecedent.

evidence.excerpt: Other firms have begun building their own AI using open-source models, which are tailored to their specific needs and trained on in-house data.
evidence.locator: Section 'Expensive frontier models have firms looking elsewhere'
evidence.explanation: Reported substitution is a possible response to expensive access. This secondary reporting does not establish survival of the stipulated startup group.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: Matched records must identify discount-dependent startups independently of later failure, establish higher effective prices for comparable workloads, and document continued Big Tech support for their providers. Inability to sustain operations caused by those increases despite that support would support the forecast. Evidence that continued provider support preserved viable operations in the identified group after discounts ended would contradict it.
